studies.title: Neural processes associated with antisaccade task performance investigated with event-related FMRI.
studies.abstract: One of the hallmarks of cognitive control is the suppression of prepotent but inappropriate responses. Here we used event-related functional MRI to measure functional brain activation during a stimulus-response incompatibility task. Subjects were instructed before a stimulus appeared either to look at the stimulus (prosaccade) or to look away from the stimulus (antisaccade). Eye movements were recorded so that functional brain activation could be grouped into prosaccades, correct antisaccades, and errors (saccades toward the stimulus on antisaccade trials). Correct antisaccade trials were associated with significantly more activation in frontal and parietal cortical areas compared with prosaccade trials during the late preparatory period before stimulus appearance. Correct antisaccades evoked more activation than errors in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and presupplementary eye fields during this period. No significant differences were found for any comparisons early in the preparatory period. Our data suggest that the preparation of an antisaccade activates a large frontal and parietal network that may be involved in presetting the oculomotor system for the antisaccade task. These findings indicate that a large network of frontal and posterior areas is modulated during the latter component of the preparatory period on antisaccade compared with prosaccade trials. The results further suggest that the activation level of frontal cortical areas before stimulus presentation is associated with subjects' performance in the antisaccade task. In contrast, we found no areas that were more active for correct antisaccades than prosaccades or for correct antisaccades than error antisaccades during the stimulus-response period. In fact, a number of posterior cortical areas and a few areas in the superior frontal lobe were more active during the stimulus-response period on prosaccade trials than on antisaccade trials. Error antisaccades showed a larger activation in the ACC during the stimulus-response period compared with correct antisaccades.

studies.title: Effector-specific fields for motor preparation in the human frontal cortex.
studies.abstract: We investigated the neural correlates of advance motor preparation in two experiments that required a movement in response to a peripheral visual stimulus. In one experiment (the memory delay paradigm), subjects knew the target location during a preparatory 'memory delay' interval; in the other experiment they did not know the target location during a 'gap period' (the gap paradigm). In both experiments we further varied the effector that was instructed, either the eye or the forelimb. An area that codes motor preparation should exhibit increases during the memory delay and gap period and such increases should predict some attribute of performance (planning to use the eye or the forelimb). We first identified the frontoparietal visuomotor areas using standard fMRI block designs. Subjects were then scanned using event-related fMRI. With the exception of primary motor cortex (M1), all areas (putative lateral intraparietal area (putLIP), dorsal premotor cortex (PMd), frontal eye field (FEF), ventral frontal eye field (FEFv), supplementary motor area (SMA)) showed gap and memory delay activation for both saccades and pointing. Gap activity in the frontal areas was higher than in the parietal area(s) investigated. The observation that 'memory delay' activity was equivalent or less than gap activity in all areas suggests that what is commonly considered to be memory-related responses largely represents advance motor preparation. Certain areas showed increased activation during the gap or memory delay intervals for pointing (PMd, FEF, FEFv) or saccades (SMA, putLIP). These observations suggest an important role of the frontal cortex in advance motor preparation.

studies.title: The posterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortex mediate the anticipatory allocation of spatial attention.
studies.abstract: The purpose of this study was to identify brain regions underlying internally generated anticipatory biases toward locations where significant events are expected to occur. Subjects fixated centrally and responded to peripheral targets preceded by a spatially valid (predictive), invalid (misleading), or neutral central cue while undergoing fMRI scanning. In some validly cued trials, reaction time was significantly shorter than in trials with neutral cues, indicating that the cue had successfully induced a spatial redistribution of motivational valence, manifested as expectancy. The largest cue benefits led to selectively greater activations within the posterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortex. These two areas thus appear to establish a neural interface between attention and motivation. An inverse relationship to cue benefit was seen in the parietal cortex, suggesting that spatial expectancy may entail the inhibition of attention-related areas to reduce distractibility by events at irrelevant locations.

studies.title: Neural mechanisms involved in error processing: a comparison of errors made with and without awareness.
studies.abstract: The ability to detect an error in one's own performance and then to improve ongoing performance based on this error processing is critical for effective behaviour. In our event-related fMRI experiment, we show that explicit awareness of a response inhibition commission error and subsequent post-error behaviour were associated with bilateral prefrontal and parietal brain activation. Activity in the anterior cingulate region, typically associated with error detection, was equivalent for both errors subjects were aware of and those they were not aware of making. While anterior cingulate activation has repeatedly been associated with error-related processing, these results suggest that, in isolation, it is not sufficient for conscious awareness of errors or post-error adaptation of response strategies. Instead, it appears, irrespective of awareness, to detect information about stimuli/responses that requires interpretation in other brain regions for strategic implementation of post-error adjustments of behaviour.

studies.title: Contextual interference in recognition memory with age.
studies.abstract: Previous behavioral research suggests that although elderly adults' memory benefits from supportive context, misleading or irrelevant contexts produce greater interference. In the present study, we use event-related fMRI to investigate age differences when processing contextual information to make recognition judgments. Twenty-one young and twenty elderly incidentally encoded pictures of objects presented in meaningful contexts, and completed a memory test for the objects presented in identical or novel contexts. Elderly committed more false alarms than young when novel objects were presented in familiar, but task-irrelevant, contexts. Elderly showed reduced engagement of bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate relative to young, reflecting disruption of a cognitive control network for processing context with age. Disruption occurred for both high and low-performing elderly, suggesting that cognitive control deficits are pervasive with age. Despite showing disruption of the cognitive control network, high-performing elderly recruited additional middle and medial frontal regions that were not recruited by either low-performing elderly or young adults. This suggests that high-performing elderly may compensate for the disruption of the cognitive control network by recruiting additional frontal resources to overcome cognitive control deficits that affect recognition memory.

studies.title: All for one but not one for all: how multiple number representations are recruited in one numerical task.
studies.abstract: Number processing recruits a complex network of multiple numerical representations. Usually the components of this network are examined in a between-task approach with the disadvantage of relying upon different instructions, tasks, and inhomogeneous stimulus sets across different studies. A within-task approach may avoid these disadvantages and access involved numerical representations more specifically. In the present study we employed a within-task approach to investigate numerical representations activated in the number bisection task (NBT) using parametric rapid event-related fMRI. Participants were to judge whether the central number of a triplet was also its arithmetic mean (e.g. 23_26_29) or not (e.g. 23_25_29). Activation in the left inferior parietal cortex was associated with the deployment of arithmetic fact knowledge, while activation of the intraparietal cortex indicated more intense magnitude processing, instrumental aspects of calculation and integration of the base-10 structure of two-digit numbers. These results replicate evidence from the literature. Furthermore, activation in the dorsolateral and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex revealed mechanisms of feature monitoring and inhibition as well as allocation of cognitive resources recruited to solve a specific triplet. We conclude that the network of numerical representations should rather be studied in a within-task approach than in varying between-task approaches.

studies.title: Prefrontal cortex guides context-appropriate responding during language production.
studies.abstract: Although language processing is thought to frequently require cognitive control, little is known about the cognitive and neural basis of the control of language. Here, we demonstrate that processing of context by the PFC plays an important role in the control of language comprehension and production. Using a missing letter paradigm and fMRI, we found that increased activation in the PFC (but not in posterior regions), while encoding and maintaining context information, predicted context-appropriate responses. Furthermore, greater selection demands increased activity during responding in the same regions engaged during the encoding and maintenance of context. Overall, as in other cognitive task domains, these results suggest that PFC context processing plays an important role in the control of language.

studies.title: Differential engagement of anterior cingulate cortex subdivisions for cognitive and emotional function.
studies.abstract: Functional differentiation of dorsal (dACC) and rostral (rACC) anterior cingulate cortex for cognitive and emotional function has received considerable indirect support. Using fMRI, parallel tasks, and within-subject analysis, the present study directly tested the proposed specialization of ACC subdivisions. A Task x Region interaction confirmed more dACC activation during color-word distractors and more rACC activation during emotion-word distractors. Activity in ACC subdivisions differentially predicted behavioral performance. Connectivity with prefrontal and limbic regions also supported distinct dACC and rACC roles. Findings provide direct evidence for differential engagement of ACC subdivisions in cognitive and emotional processing and for differential functional connectivity in the implementation of cognitive control and emotion regulation. Results point to an anatomical and functional continuum rather than segregated operations.

studies.title: The neural bases of cognitive conflict and control in moral judgment.
studies.abstract: Traditional theories of moral psychology emphasize reasoning and "higher cognition," while more recent work emphasizes the role of emotion. The present fMRI data support a theory of moral judgment according to which both "cognitive" and emotional processes play crucial and sometimes mutually competitive roles. The present results indicate that brain regions associated with abstract reasoning and cognitive control (including dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex) are recruited to resolve difficult personal moral dilemmas in which utilitarian values require "personal" moral violations, violations that have previously been associated with increased activity in emotion-related brain regions. Several regions of frontal and parietal cortex predict intertrial differences in moral judgment behavior, exhibiting greater activity for utilitarian judgments. We speculate that the controversy surrounding utilitarian moral philosophy reflects an underlying tension between competing subsystems in the brain.

studies.title: When visual perception causes feeling: enhanced cross-modal processing in grapheme-color synesthesia.
studies.abstract: In synesthesia, stimulation of one sensory modality (e.g., hearing) triggers a percept in another, non-stimulated sensory modality (e.g., vision). Likewise, perception of a form (e.g., a letter) may induce a color percept (i.e., grapheme-color synesthesia). To date, the neural mechanisms underlying synesthesia remain to be elucidated. We disclosed by fMRI, while controlling for surface color processing, enhanced activity in the left intraparietal cortex during the experience of grapheme-color synesthesia (n = 9). In contrast, the perception of surface color per se activated the color centers in the fusiform gyrus bilaterally. The data support theoretical accounts that grapheme-color synesthesia may originate from enhanced cross-modal binding of form and color. A mismatch of surface color and grapheme induced synesthetically felt color additionally activated the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). This suggests that cognitive control processes become active to resolve the perceptual conflict resulting from synesthesia.

studies.title: Challenge-driven attention: interacting frontal and brainstem systems.
studies.abstract: The world is an unpredictable place, presenting challenges that fluctuate from moment to moment. However, the neural systems for responding to such challenges are far from fully understood. Using fMRI, we studied an audiovisual task in which the trials' difficulty and onset times varied unpredictably. Two regions were found to increase their activation for challenging trials, with their activities strongly correlated: right frontal cortex and the brainstem. The frontal area matched regions found in previous human studies of cognitive control, and activated in a graded manner with increasing task difficulty. The brainstem responded only to the most difficult trials, showing a phasic activity pattern paralleling locus coeruleus recordings in monkeys. These results reveal a bridge between animal and human studies, and suggest interacting roles for the brainstem and right frontal cortex: the brainstem may signal that an attentional challenge is occurring, while right frontal cortex allocates cognitive resources in response.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: fMRI study in an English peer-reviewed journal examining cognitive control/executive function (right frontal cortex activation with task difficulty). The abstract does not explicitly state participants were healthy adults, so include for full-text review to confirm I2.
studies.fulltext_screening_reason: This is an empirical task-based fMRI study that probes attentional/cognitive-control processes (challenge-driven attention), operationalized via an audiovisual simultaneity detection task that requires sustained/vigilant allocation of resources under unpredictability. The paper reports within-group, voxelwise, second-level random-effects analyses (difficulty-weighted contrasts and task vs null), with whole-brain voxelwise maps (despite partial slice coverage: 21 axial slices). Results are reported in text and figures and include MNI coordinates and ROI analyses. Participants were a within-group sample of healthy adults (n=12). Thus the study meets the meta-analysis requirements for an fMRI task assessing executive/cognitive-control-related vigilance, provides voxelwise group-level activation maps, includes within-group contrasts, and reports whole-brain results in the manuscript.

studies.title: Dissociable contributions of the mid-ventrolateral frontal cortex and the medial temporal lobe system to human memory.
studies.abstract: Although the prefrontal cortex and regions of the medial temporal lobe are commonly co-activated in neuroimaging studies, their precise respective contributions to human memory remain unclear. In this event-related fMRI study, conditions requiring volunteers to simply look at pictures of abstract art were compared with conditions in which they were explicitly instructed to remember similar stimuli for later recognition. Looking, with no explicit instruction to remember, was associated with significant increases in signal intensity in the medial temporal lobe in 19 of the 20 volunteers scanned, but not in a region of the mid-ventrolateral prefrontal cortex that has previously been implicated in memory encoding and retrieval. Behavioral data collected outside the scanner on the same task revealed that recognition of these stimuli was, however, above chance. When the task instructions were changed to encourage the volunteers to remember the stimuli, significant increases in signal intensity were observed bilaterally, in the mid-ventrolateral frontal cortex, but there was no concomitant increase within the medial temporal lobe region. Moreover, behavioral data collected outside the scanner confirmed that recognition of these stimuli was significantly improved relative to the 'just look' trials. These results suggest that the mid-ventrolateral frontal cortex and the medial temporal lobe region make dissociable contributions to human memory that correspond closely to 'top-down' and 'bottom-up' notions of cognitive control, respectively.

studies.title: Prefrontal contributions to domain-general executive control processes during temporal context retrieval.
studies.abstract: Neuroimaging studies have reported increased prefrontal cortex (PFC) activity during temporal context retrieval versus recognition memory. However, it remains unclear if these activations reflect PFC contributions to domain-general executive control processes or domain-specific retrieval processes. To gain a better understanding of the functional roles of these various PFC regions during temporal context retrieval we propose it is necessary to examine PFC activity across tasks from different domains, in which parallel manipulations are included targeting specific cognitive processes. In the current fMRI study, we examined domain-general and domain-specific PFC contributions to temporal context retrieval by increasing stimulus (but maintaining response number) and increasing response number (but maintaining stimulus number) across temporal context memory and ordering control tasks, for faces. The control task required subjects to order faces from youngest to oldest. Our behavioral results indicate that the combination of increased stimulus and response numbers significantly increased task difficulty for temporal context retrieval and ordering tasks. Across domains, increasing stimulus number, while maintaining response numbers, caused greater right lateral premotor cortex (BA 6/8) activity; whereas increasing response number, while maintaining stimulus number, caused greater domain-general left DLPFC (BA 9) and VLPFC (BA 44/45) activity. In addition, we found domain-specific right DLPFC (BA 9) activity only during retrieval events. These results highlight the functional heterogeneity of frontal cortex, and suggest its involvement in temporal context retrieval is related to its role in various cognitive control processes.

fulltext_screening_results.reason: This is an empirical fMRI and PET study using the Tower of London planning task (an established executive function domain: planning). The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I5, I6, I7, I8, I9, and I10. No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) are met.

No exclusion criteria from the list explicitly apply (e.g., the paper does include voxelwise receptor mapping and SVC, but that is not a task-evoked voxelwise activation). Full text appears complete.

Within-group task contrasts are reported and interpreted; results include conjunction and regression analyses. Participants are a within-group sample of healthy volunteers. Therefore it satisfies all inclusion criteria (I5, I6, I7, I8, I9, I10). No exclusion criteria apply (no ROI-only, no connectivity-only, no only between-group contrasts, and it is empirical). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion, references).

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study of executive function (attention switching within verbal working memory). Within-group contrasts are reported (task vs rest and parametric modulation by switching frequency). Participants are a healthy adult sample. Reporting includes tables/figures of whole-brain results. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only contrasts, or non-empirical paper) are violated. Therefore all inclusion criteria I5–I10 are met.

Contrasts include RST versus control and RST versus read within HSS and LSS groups. Methods, results, and discussion are complete in the full text. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion criteria.

This is an empirical event-related fMRI study of the Wisconsin Card Sorting Task, which assesses cognitive flexibility (an executive function). The paper reports group-level, voxelwise within-group contrasts (multiple WCST event types vs control) with whole-brain voxelwise statistical maps and multiple-comparison correction, and peak coordinates/tables are provided. Participant group (healthy adults) is acceptable. The full text includes methods, results, and discussion. Thus all required inclusion criteria are satisfied (I5,I6,I7,I8,I9,I10) and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical, task-based fMRI study of an executive function paradigm (random number generation). The paper reports group-level, voxelwise SPM99 analyses (paired-samples t-tests per voxel) with statistical parametric maps and cluster coordinates for RNG minus counting, satisfying whole-brain voxelwise reporting. At least one within-group task contrast is presented (RNG vs counting; 1 Hz and 2 Hz conditions). Participants are a healthy group (acceptable per I9). No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity/resting-state-only, not only between-group contrasts, and it is empirical). This is an empirical task-based fMRI study of working memory (an executive function) in healthy adults. This is an empirical task-based PET study using [11C]raclopride during the Montreal Card Sorting Task (MCST), probing planning/set-shifting (executive functions). Results are reported with coordinates and figures; analyses are not ROI-only, connectivity-only, or solely between-group contrasts. Full article text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is present. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria and violates no exclusion criteria.

Therefore it satisfies the meta-analysis inclusion requirements for fMRI task-based executive function, working memory domain, whole-brain voxelwise results, within-group contrasts, and permissible participant groups. Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical PET meta-analysis that reanalyzes 63 subjects and 370 spatially normalized PET scans from nine task protocols using voxelwise SPM conjunction analysis. It includes within-group REST vs TASK contrasts (185 pairs of REST/TASK scans), reports whole-brain voxelwise results and stereotactic coordinates, and specifically addresses working memory and executive-function-related processes. Therefore it meets the review’s requirements: PET task-based paradigm (I5); contains tasks within executive domains (e.g., spatial working memory, manipulation/inhibition components) (I6); provides group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses (I7); includes within-group task contrasts (I8); includes an eligible participant group (healthy adults) (I9); and reports whole-brain results/coordinates in text/tables (I10). No exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is a task-based fMRI study of non-perceptual attentional set-shifting (cognitive flexibility), meeting the review objective. The paper reports group-level, voxelwise SPM96 analyses (conjunctions and contrasts such as A–R, A–T, A–W, A–L) with whole-brain statistical thresholding and coordinates described. It reports within-group task contrasts (task vs rest and condition subtractions), uses healthy adult participants, and presents whole-brain results in the text (with coordinates). It is empirical and not ROI-only or connectivity-only. Full article content (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is provided. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an event-related fMRI task study of somatosensory Go/Nogo paradigms that directly assess executive functions (response execution/inhibition and counting/working memory). The paper reports group-level, voxelwise whole-brain analyses (SPM2 random-effects), thresholding and coordinates, and within-group task contrasts (Movement Go, Count Go, Movement Go vs Count Go, Go vs Nogo contrasts). Participants are a within-group healthy adult sample and results are reported in text and coordinates. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity/rest-only, not only between-group contrasts, and is empirical). The provided full text contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion and appears complete. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis objective.

This is a task-based fMRI study of planning using the Tower of London (an executive function task). The paper reports voxelwise, whole-brain random-effects SPM analyses (main effect of task, easy vs difficult, and within-group effects for males and females) with thresholding and tables/figures, and includes within-group contrasts (task > control/rest). Participants are healthy adults and the full article text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is provided. The study is not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, and not a non-empirical paper. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria and violates no exclusion criteria.

This is a task-based fMRI study assessing spatial working memory via a memory-guided saccade (MGS) task, which falls within executive function domains (working memory) and meets I5 and I6. The paper reports voxelwise, group-level whole-brain analyses (MGS vs VGS contrast) with standardized-space group maps despite partial slice coverage, satisfying I7. A within-group task contrast (MGS-VGS) is explicitly used and reported, satisfying I8. Participant groups (adolescent high-risk offspring and healthy controls) are acceptable per I9. Whole-brain results are described in the text and figures, meeting I10. No exclusion criteria apply: this is not an ROI-only study (E3), not connectivity/rest-only (E4), and it reports within-group contrasts rather than only between-group contrasts (E5). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an event-related and blocked-design fMRI study that explicitly investigates executive functions (attention-switching and response inhibition) using task-based paradigms. The paper reports within-group, voxelwise, random-effects whole-brain analyses (switch−nonswitch; incompatible−compatible; High-Switch−Low-Switch) with FDR correction and provides peak coordinates/tables and figures. Participants are a human within-group sample (undergraduates). Results are reported at the group level and voxelwise and thus meet the meta-analysis requirements. Full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion.

Although this paper uses fMRI with group-level, voxelwise within-group contrasts (black faces > baseline; black > white) and reports whole-brain coordinates, it does not implement an explicit executive-function task in the scanner. The fMRI paradigm was a spatial-location perceptual task (indicating left/right presentation of faces); the Stroop inhibitory task (an established executive function assay) was administered behaviorally in a separate session outside the scanner. Therefore the study does not meet the key inclusion requirements that (I5) the fMRI/PET study assesses executive function or cognitive control using a task-based paradigm in the scanner, and (I6) the in-scanner task fall within established executive function domains (working memory, inhibition, cognitive flexibility, planning, vigilance, initiation). Met inclusion criteria: I7 (whole-brain voxelwise analysis reported), I8 (within-group task contrasts reported), I9 (participant group acceptable), I10 (whole-brain results reported as coordinates/figures). No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply. Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study of working memory (n-back), an executive function domain. The paper reports multiple within-group, voxelwise group-level contrasts (1-back vs 0-back, 2-back vs 0-back, 2-back vs 1-back) analyzed with SPM and whole-brain correction, with tables and figures of activations. Whole-brain, group random-effects analyses are described. Thus it provides qualifying task activation maps for inclusion in a meta-analysis of executive function task activations. Full text is complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). No exclusion criteria are met.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study using an n-back working memory task (executive function). The paper reports group- and within-subject voxelwise SPM99 analyses (random-effects ANOVAs), with whole-brain voxelwise contrasts (on-periods vs off-periods) and reported activation coordinates and clusters. Although slice coverage excluded the cerebellum, analyses were voxelwise rather than ROI-restricted. Results include within-group task activation maps for participants (MDMA users and controls) and coordinates are reported in the text and figures. Thus all inclusion criteria (I5,I6,I7,I8,I9,I10) are satisfied, and none of the exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an empirical fMRI study of working memory (an executive function). Methods report task-based paradigms (phonological and visual working memory) with within-group, voxelwise group-level analyses using SPM99 (fixed-effects), reporting voxelwise significance (P<0.05 corrected) and figures/tables of whole-brain activations. Although acquisition used 16 slices (partial coverage), analyses were voxelwise and group-level contrasts (memory vs matched control) are reported. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met (I5,I6,I7,I8,I9,I10). No exclusion criteria are triggered (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not only between-group contrasts, and not non-empirical). Full text appears to contain introduction, methods, results, and discussion (core content present).

This is a task-based fMRI study of spatial working memory (an executive function domain). The paper reports group-level voxelwise analyses (Z-maps, FDR correction), one-sample t-tests and mixed-effect ANOVA for within-group contrasts (maintenance vs recognition; modality comparisons), and whole-brain results reported in text/maps. Participant group is healthy adults; within-group contrasts are provided. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. No exclusion criteria are met.

This is an empirical, task-based fMRI study that used a validated spatial working memory (Visual Delayed Matching to Sample) paradigm (executive function domain: working memory). The paper reports voxelwise, group-level SPM2 analyses (whole-brain voxelwise contrasts) isolating the working-memory component (4s minus 1s delay) and reports coordinates/tables and figures of activation. At least one within-group task contrast (delay 4 > delay 1 / task vs matching) is reported. Participant group (healthy postmenopausal women) is acceptable. Results are presented in tables and figures. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity/resting-only, not only between-group contrasts). Full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion, so is complete.

Full text appears incomplete (only title/abstract/metadata provided). From the abstract it is clear this is an event-related fMRI GO/NOGO task addressing inhibition and cognitive control, so inclusion criteria I5 and I6 are satisfied. However the supplied content does not allow confirmation of required whole-brain, group-level voxelwise task-evoked maps (I7) or explicit within-group task contrasts (I8). Recommend obtaining the complete article to confirm I7 and I8 (and I10, if relevant).

This paper reports an event-related fMRI study of working memory (an executive function domain) in healthy adults, with task-based within-group contrasts and group random-effects (voxelwise) analyses and reported stereotactic coordinates and whole-brain maps. The full text contains introduction, methods (including whole-brain acquisition and GLM/group analyses), results, and discussion, so the article meets all inclusion criteria and violates no exclusion criteria.

This is an empirical fMRI study using a go/no-go task (inhibition), an established executive function domain. The paper reports within-group task contrasts (Table 1) and exploratory whole-brain, voxelwise between-group analyses (Table 3) using SPM2, with results reported in tables/figures. Therefore it meets I5 (task-based fMRI), I6 (inhibition task), I7 (whole-brain voxelwise analyses reported), I8 (within-group task contrasts), I9 (clinical participant groups allowed), and I10 (results reported as tables/coordinates). No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity/resting-only, includes within-group contrasts, empirical data). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Inclusion is appropriate for a meta-analysis pooling executive-function task activations across groups.

This is a task-based fMRI study of auditory verbal working memory (an executive function). The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion, and reports voxelwise, group-level SPM analyses (within-group WM vs vigilance contrasts and whole-brain/random-effects analyses). Partial-brain acquisition (15 axial slices) is present but voxelwise analyses were performed, satisfying whole-brain/voxelwise requirement. Within-group contrasts are reported for groups. No exclusion criteria are met.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study of planning (Tower of London), an established executive function domain. The full text contains methods, results, and discussion. The study reports voxelwise t-maps (per-voxel activation thresholds) and presents group-averaged activation patterns (figures/tables), satisfying the requirement for a voxelwise task-evoked map despite partial slice coverage. Within-group contrasts are reported (task vs baseline and difficulty-parametric contrasts) and group-level statistics (ANOVAs on activation measures) are presented. Participants are a within-group healthy sample and individual-difference correlations are reported. Results are reported in figures and tables. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not only between-group contrasts, and not non-empirical). Therefore all inclusion criteria I5, I6, I7, I8, I9 and I10 are met.

This is an event-related task-based fMRI study of cognitive switching (cognitive flexibility), an executive function domain. It reports a within-group, voxelwise group analysis (group‐level GBAM produced via permutation testing and cluster-level inference) contrasting switch vs repeat trials (a within-group task contrast). Whole-brain acquisition and analyses are described, with results reported in text, tables, and figures. Participants are healthy adults but inclusion accepts any participant groups. Therefore inclusion criteria I5, I6, I7, I8, I9, and I10 are met. No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply. The provided full text includes introduction, methods, results, discussion, and conclusions, so full text appears complete.

This is an empirical event-related fMRI study using Go/No-go tasks to probe response inhibition and working memory (executive function). It reports group-level, voxelwise random-effects analyses (corrected P≤0.05) with whole-brain coverage for many subjects, presents within-group task contrasts (Go vs No-go, No-go vs Go, conjunctions), and reports results as tables/figures/coordinates. The full article includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Thus it meets inclusion criteria I5, I6, I7, I8, I9, and I10, and violates no exclusion criteria. Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical fMRI study that reports within-group, voxelwise task activation contrasts probing executive resources (working memory and planning/decision-making) during sentence disambiguation. The authors performed random-effects, whole-brain SPM2 analyses and present voxelwise contrasts (e.g., less-consistent vs more-consistent; with WM vs without WM) with coordinates and figures. The task manipulations fall squarely within executive function domains (working memory and planning), and group-level voxelwise results are reported. The full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, and appendices, so the full text appears complete. Therefore all required inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This article reports an empirical task-based fMRI study of planning (Tower of London), an executive function, with both within-group (TOL vs fixation) and group-level voxelwise analyses (SPM99). The methods describe whole-brain preprocessing and group random-effects contrasts, and results include within-group activation maps, tables of coordinates, and figures. Partial slice coverage was used but voxelwise analyses were performed (acceptable per protocol). Thus it satisfies all inclusion criteria for task-based fMRI executive function studies (I5–I10). No exclusion criteria apply (no ROI-only, no connectivity-only, not non-empirical, and within-group contrasts are reported). Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is a task-based PET study of the Tower of London planning task (an established executive function domain: planning). The paper reports group-level, voxelwise whole-brain analyses (t-statistic images, Gaussian random field correction), with within-group contrasts (EXPT1 vs control, EXPT10 vs control) and regression analyses relating rCBF to performance. Whole-brain results are described with coordinates and peaks. Participants are healthy adults. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion (not truncated). Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical PET activation study using the Tower of London planning task (an established executive function: planning). The full text contains Introduction, Methods (PET acquisition, SPM voxelwise preprocessing and statistical analyses), Results (group-level category contrast: planning vs rest; correlation analyses of complexity and movement; tables/figures of whole-brain SPM results), and Discussion. The study reports within-group voxelwise task contrasts (planning minus rest and parametric correlations) suitable for inclusion. Whole-brain voxelwise analyses are performed and reported; partial brain coverage (field-of-view note) does not preclude inclusion per review criteria. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, only between-group contrasts, or non-empirical) are met. Therefore the study meets all required inclusion criteria (I5–I10) and should be included.

This is an empirical, task-based fMRI study manipulating executive demand (two-back vs one-back; source vs item memory). It reports within-group, voxelwise whole-brain analyses (SPM random-effects) and provides coordinates and conjunction results for sustained and transient load contrasts. Tasks include a canonical executive domain (working memory) and episodic source memory with executive control demands. Group-level contrasts (high vs low load) are reported and thresholded, satisfying the meta-analysis requirements. Full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only, or non-empirical) are met.

The study is an fMRI task-based investigation of working memory (an executive function) with within-group task vs control contrasts, and reports voxelwise activation coordinates. However, the paper does not clearly present a group-level, voxelwise task-evoked statistical map (I7). Analyses are described as voxelwise at the individual-subject level with reported per-subject peaks and averaged coordinates, but no explicit group-level voxelwise statistical map is reported. Therefore it fails to meet inclusion criterion I7, so it must be excluded. The full text appears complete.

This is an empirical PET neuroimaging study that used a task-based Operation Span dual-task (working memory) paradigm targeting executive components (task-switching and storage-during-distraction). Group-level, voxelwise analyses are reported (subtraction images averaged across subjects, t-statistics computed voxelwise with multiple-comparison correction), with whole-brain results presented in figures and tables of stereotaxic coordinates. The paper reports within-group task contrasts (Operation Span vs. Math and Memory, Math vs. Control, Memory vs. Control) for young and senior groups. Results are reported as coordinates/tables and ROI analyses. Therefore it satisfies inclusion criteria I5–I10 and does not meet any exclusion criteria. Full text is complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion present).

The full text reports an empirical, task-based fMRI study using an established executive-function task (n-back working memory) with both clinical (cocaine abusers) and control groups. The paper describes whole-brain, voxelwise analyses (SPM2 two-way voxel-by-voxel repeated-measures ANOVA), and reports within-group contrasts (1-back vs 0-back; 2-back vs 0-back; WM-load 2-back vs 1-back) as well as group comparisons. Results are reported across the brain (tables/figures of activation clusters and coordinates). Thus all inclusion criteria I5–I10 are satisfied and no exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study of working memory (syllable working memory) in healthy Japanese adults. It assesses an executive function domain (working memory) using block-designed task contrasts and reports within-group voxelwise analyses (task vs rest and l/r vs b/n or d/n) using SPM99, with activation maps and coordinate tables provided. Thus it provides whole-brain, group-level voxelwise task-evoked results. All required inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion, figures/tables, references).

Full text appears incomplete (only title/abstract provided). This is an empirical PET study using a task-based executive function paradigm (self-ordered object working memory). The task falls squarely within the working memory domain (executive function). Participants are a healthy adult sample and results are reported as coordinates and described in text. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not only between-group contrasts, and not non-empirical). The provided full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion, so the full text appears complete. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria and none of the exclusions.

This is an empirical PET study using a task-based paradigm that directly assesses visual working memory, an established executive function domain. Group-level voxelwise analyses were performed in SPM99 with multiple within-group contrasts reported (e.g., SPA–AM, NSPA–AM, SPA–NSPA) and stereotaxic coordinates and statistical thresholds provided (whole-brain voxelwise results and figures/tables). Participant sample and methods are described in full (introduction, methods, results, discussion). Therefore all inclusion criteria for task activations (I5,I6,I7,I8,I9,I10) are met, and no exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical, task-based fMRI study using an audiospatial n-back paradigm (working memory) that clearly falls within executive function domains. Although slice coverage is partial, analyses are voxelwise (qualifies under I7). No exclusion criteria are met.

Full text appears to be incomplete (only title/abstract/metadata available). This is an empirical task-based fMRI study of cognitive control using a stop-signal (inhibition) paradigm in healthy adults. Full text includes introduction, methods, results, discussion, and conclusions. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis objective.

This fMRI study directly assesses an executive function (attention switching/cognitive flexibility within working memory) using task-based paradigms (verbal, visuospatial, combined). It reports group-level, voxelwise whole-brain analyses (one-sample t-tests vs rest; voxelwise ANOVAs; parametric High>Medium>Low switching contrasts) with cluster-correction, satisfying voxelwise whole-brain evidence. This is an empirical task-based fMRI study that examines executive domains (2-back working memory and sustained attention/vigilance) using Arterial Spin Labeling. The paper reports group-level, voxelwise GLM random-effects analyses with whole-brain multislice coverage and cluster-level inference comparing each task to a resting baseline (within-group contrasts). Results are presented in tables, figures, and text (activation peak coordinates and %CBF changes). Participants are healthy adults (within-group contrasts reported). No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not only between-group contrasts, and not non-empirical). Full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion.

This is an empirical PET study using task-based paradigms probing executive functions (spatial working memory and planning) in healthy volunteers. Tasks fall squarely within executive domains (working memory, planning). Participant sample and within-group contrasts are clearly described. No exclusion criteria apply: results are not ROI-only, not solely connectivity or resting-state, and not only between-group contrasts. This is an empirical task-based fMRI study using an emotional counting Stroop, a well-established inhibition/cognitive-control (executive function) paradigm. The paper reports group-level voxelwise nonparametric (KS) statistical maps and provides coordinates and corrected p-values for within-group contrasts (negative vs neutral; fixation vs task), satisfying whole-brain voxelwise reporting even though slice coverage was partial. Participants are a within-group sample of healthy adults and results are presented in text/figures/tables. All inclusion criteria for the review are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study using an n-back working memory paradigm (an established executive function). The paper reports voxelwise, group-level SPM99 analyses (random-effects), whole-brain EPI coverage, and reports significant activations with MNI coordinates and renderings. Within-group contrasts (linear memory-load contrasts and main effects of memory load; memory load × stimulus interaction) are presented for the participant group. This paper reports original task-based fMRI data using well-established executive function paradigms (n-back working memory and the Iowa Gambling Task). It includes within-group contrasts (1/2/3-back vs 0-back; gambling vs control) and reports group-level voxelwise analyses using SPM99 with whole-brain statistical mapping and corrected thresholds. The n-back clearly falls within the executive domain (working memory), satisfying task-domain requirements; the IGT provides additional decision-making-related activation. The full text includes Introduction, Methods (acquisition and voxelwise analysis), Results (within-group activation maps and parametric analysis), and Discussion, so the full text appears complete. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, only between-group contrasts, or non-empirical) are met.

Although this is a task-based fMRI study with whole-brain, voxelwise, within-group contrasts and reports group-level results (meeting I5, I7, I8, I9, I10), the experimental paradigm focuses on motor timing and sensorimotor transfer (continuation tapping and shift of effector) rather than canonical executive functions (working memory, inhibition, cognitive flexibility as commonly operationalized, planning, vigilance, initiation). This is an empirical task-based fMRI study using a go/no-go paradigm (response inhibition) that falls within executive function (inhibition). The paper reports within-group, voxelwise, whole-brain group analyses (generic brain activation maps and condition contrasts: no-go vs go) with tables and figures of whole-brain results for each condition (sham and ATD). Participants are healthy volunteers (eligible under I9). Results are reported as group-level voxelwise contrasts and coordinates. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion, references).

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study of response inhibition (Go/NoGo) in typically developing participants (ages 8–20). The paper reports voxelwise, group-level whole-brain analyses (SPM99) including within-group contrasts (NoGo minus Go) and voxelwise age-regression maps (positive and negative correlations). Results are reported in the main text (and likely tables/figures). Thus it meets all inclusion criteria for task domain (inhibition), imaging modality and task paradigm (I5,I6), whole-brain voxelwise analyses (I7), a within-group task contrast (I8), inclusion of a developmental participant group (I9), and reporting of whole-brain results in text/figures (I10). No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity/resting-only, not only between-group contrasts, and is an empirical study). Full text appears complete.

This is a task-based fMRI study using an n-back working memory paradigm (executive domain) with healthy participants. The full text reports group-level, voxelwise whole-brain analyses (one-sample t-test random-effects for 2-back vs 0-back and between-group ANOVA), including tables and figures of activations and cluster statistics. A within-group task contrast (2-back vs 0-back) is explicitly reported. The paper is empirical and contains complete sections (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion). Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria (I5–I10) and violates no exclusion criteria.

This is an empirical PET study using a task-based paradigm that explicitly manipulates working memory updating (an executive function). The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion (not just abstract/metadata). This is a task-based fMRI study using a 2-back working memory paradigm (executive function domain), with group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (SPM2, FDR-corrected) and multiple within-group task contrasts (e.g., Binding, Sign, Speech vs rest; Sign>Speech; 2Binding>Sign+Speech). No exclusion criteria are met. Full text appears complete (includes introduction, methods, results, discussion). Appropriate for inclusion in a meta-analysis of executive function task activations.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study using the emotional Stroop (an inhibition/attention executive function task). This is an empirical, task-based fMRI study of executive function (motor inhibition, interference inhibition, cognitive flexibility) meeting the review objective. This is an empirical, task-based fMRI study reporting within-group, voxelwise, group-level contrasts for executive function tasks (Go/No-Go inhibition; also reward/loss tasks). This is an empirical task-based fMRI study of planning (an executive function) using the Tower of London paradigm. The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion.
